name: Factors Influencing Gustatory Perception
what: This subtopic examines the biological (age, genetics), psychological (appearance, food packaging, perceptual set), and social (culture) factors that influence how we perceive flavour. It builds on the mechanisms of gustatory sensation introduced in the sensation and perception subtopic.
why: Flavour perception is not determined by taste alone; it is actively shaped by who we are, what we expect, and the cultural context in which we eat. This explains why the same food can taste very different to different people.

items.title: I can explain how age acts as a biological factor that influences gustatory perception
items.what: As people age, the number of taste buds and gustatory receptors decreases, the papillae on the tongue become less sensitive, saliva production declines, and the sense of smell weakens. Together, these changes reduce the intensity of flavour perception.
items.why: Understanding age-related changes in gustatory perception explains why children are often fussier eaters than adults and why older adults may require stronger seasoning to perceive flavour at the same intensity as younger people.
items.example: A 70-year-old finding that the pie they loved at age 25 now tastes bland is likely experiencing an age-related reduction in gustatory receptor sensitivity rather than a change in the pie's recipe.

items.title: I can explain how genetics acts as a biological factor that influences gustatory perception
items.what: Genetic differences determine the number of taste buds a person inherits and their sensitivity to particular flavours. People can be classified as supertasters (highly sensitive, more taste buds), medium-tasters (average sensitivity), or non-tasters (lower sensitivity, fewer taste buds). Genetic factors also determine specific food preferences, such as whether coriander tastes pleasant or soapy.
items.why: Genetics explains why flavour preferences differ meaningfully between individuals even when they have had identical food experiences, highlighting a fundamental biological source of variation in gustatory perception.
items.example: A supertaster finds dark chocolate intensely bitter and unpleasant at 70% cocoa, while a non-taster with fewer taste buds finds the same chocolate mildly bitter and enjoyable.

items.title: I can explain how the appearance of food (colour and shape) influences gustatory perception
items.what: The colour and shape of food influence expectations about its flavour, which then shape actual perception. Colours that do not match expectations can cause people to misidentify flavours or perceive something as tasting wrong. Round shapes tend to be associated with sweetness, while angular shapes are associated with bitterness or savoury flavour.
items.why: The influence of appearance demonstrates that gustatory perception integrates information from the visual cortex, meaning what we see actively shapes what we taste.
items.example: When Cadbury changed their chocolate block from rectangular segments to rounded segments without altering the recipe, customers reported the chocolate tasted sweeter, consistent with the association between round shapes and sweetness.

items.title: I can explain how food packaging influences gustatory perception through perceptual set
items.what: Brand names, logos, images, and visual design on food packaging can influence expectations about flavour quality, freshness, or character. Familiarity with a trusted or expensive brand can lead people to perceive its products as tasting better, while packaging imagery (such as farming scenes on a juice bottle) can create associations with freshness.
items.why: Packaging effects show that gustatory perception can be altered before food is even tasted, revealing how strongly our perceptual set shapes sensory experience.
items.example: Children in a study reported that identical chips tasted better when served in a packaging they recognised as McDonald's compared to a plain white bag, demonstrating that brand recognition influenced their gustatory perception.

items.title: I can explain how perceptual set acts as a psychological factor influencing gustatory perception
items.what: A person's perceptual set for food is shaped by their historical experiences, mood, motivation, and contextual expectations. These factors prime the individual to expect certain flavours, making them more likely to perceive the flavour in line with those expectations, even if it does not fully match the actual sensory input.
items.why: Understanding perceptual set in gustatory perception explains why the context in which food is eaten can alter its perceived taste, and why our history with a food matters as much as the food's actual chemistry.
items.example: A person who has previously enjoyed a particular brand of coffee perceives a new batch from that brand as high quality before tasting it, and the positive expectation enhances their actual perception of its flavour.

items.title: I can explain how culture acts as a social factor influencing gustatory perception
items.what: The foods that are normal and familiar within a person's ethnic and social culture shape their taste preferences and their tolerance for unfamiliar flavours. Cultural values around health, socialising, or food traditions also influence how flavoursome or enjoyable food is perceived to be.
items.why: Cultural influences on taste demonstrate that gustatory perception is partly learned through social experience, which is why food preferences vary systematically across different cultural groups.
items.example: A person raised in a culture where spicy food is common from childhood perceives moderately spicy dishes as pleasant and normal, while someone from a culture with little spicy food tradition may perceive the same dish as uncomfortably intense.

items.title: I can evaluate the relative influence of biological, psychological, and social factors on gustatory perception in a given scenario
items.what: In any given scenario involving taste, multiple factors may interact simultaneously. A complete evaluation identifies which factor is most relevant, justifies why, and acknowledges how other factors may also be contributing.
items.why: Real-world gustatory experiences are rarely explained by a single factor alone; the ability to identify and weigh multiple influences is essential for complex exam-style analysis questions.
items.example: A supertaster (biological) from a health-conscious culture (social) who sees fresh produce images on a smoothie label (psychological) will have their gustatory perception shaped by all three factors at once, though the biological sensitivity may most strongly determine the intensity of what they taste.
